content:
Dear Corvale Mobility Hiring Team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor role. I bring seven years of experience in QA automation, with the last two focused primarily on CI/CD pipelines, test environments and build tooling. At Odrava Health, I own GitLab CI pipelines for three product teams of around 25 developers. By parallelising test jobs, caching dependencies and separating end-to-end testing, I reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly CI runner costs by approximately 30%.

I’ve also built short-lived merge-request environments using Docker Compose and, later, Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster. These environments include the application, PostgreSQL and seeded data, and are automatically removed after merge or inactivity. Alongside this, I maintain an end-to-end test suite of around 900 pytest and Playwright tests, built CI dashboards in Grafana, and wrote a guide to the CI system that is used in team onboarding. This work has taught me to make infrastructure useful to the teams relying on it, and to improve reliability through automation, observability and clear documentation.

My personal infrastructure projects have given me further hands-on experience with Terraform, Kubernetes and GitOps. I built a three-node k3s homelab with applications deployed through Argo CD, and set up Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik and cert-manager. I also used Terraform to provision infrastructure for a small Hetzner VPS. My professional infrastructure work has centered on CI/CD and test environments, while my Terraform and cloud work has been in personal projects.

Corvale’s work connecting a new train fleet with cloud services is an exciting infrastructure challenge. I’d welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience building and improving delivery infrastructure could contribute to the Fleet Connectivity team, while I continue developing my cloud infrastructure engineering skills.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Marta Kowal-Brandt

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, well structured, and appropriately concise. It uses strong quantified evidence: reducing pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes, reducing runner costs by approximately 30%, and maintaining approximately 900 tests. It also presents the transition from QA automation toward DevOps honestly, distinguishing professional infrastructure work from personal Terraform and cloud learning. The main content weakness is that it does not explicitly connect the candidate's evidence to several central role themes, such as technical ownership, stakeholder collaboration, observability, reliability, and system design. The closing is also somewhat cautious and emphasizes continuing to develop skills rather than clearly stating the value the candidate can already contribute.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The plain-text layout, standard greeting, readable paragraphs, and absence of tables, graphics, columns, or unusual formatting are ATS- and AI-screening-friendly. The letter includes useful terms such as Cloud Infrastructure, DevOps, CI/CD, GitLab CI, Docker Compose, Helm, Kubernetes, Terraform, GitOps, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and cert-manager. AI screening probability is good for CI/CD and test-infrastructure aspects of the role, but weaker for the job's core terms because the letter does not mention AWS, infrastructure-as-code repository ownership, systems architecture, networking, SSL/TLS, security, stakeholder alignment, or technical proposals. Only supported terms should be added: the candidate should not claim Terragrunt, mTLS, production cloud operations, or strong Terraform experience.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The letter is a credible match for CI/CD-focused infrastructure engineering and for building reliable, observable test environments. It demonstrates ownership of pipelines, measurable analytical improvement, Kubernetes-based environment delivery, monitoring, documentation, and collaboration with QA and product reviewers. It also aligns moderately with Corvale's ownership-oriented and engineering-led culture through examples of owning delivery infrastructure and improving processes for multiple teams. However, the candidate's material shows important role-fit gaps: no Terragrunt, no demonstrated mTLS or broader network design, no confirmed production AWS or other major-cloud operations, no IoT/automotive or remote-device integration, and no clear backend/full-stack experience. The letter should make the supported transferable evidence more explicit without presenting these gaps as existing expertise.
critique.improvement_instructions:
PRIORITY IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the second paragraph, make stakeholder collaboration explicit using evidence already in the candidate material. After the sentence about ephemeral environments, add a sentence such as: "The environments enabled QA and product reviewers to examine features before merge, with end-to-end tests running against each environment." This directly supports the requirement to bring stakeholders along and shows that the infrastructure served multiple teams.
2. In the second paragraph, strengthen the leadership and communication evidence without overstating formal leadership. Revise the sentence beginning "Alongside this, I maintain..." to include: "I also wrote the internal CI guide used for team onboarding and mentored two QA interns." This supports technical ownership, clear communication, and knowledge sharing.
3. In the third paragraph, clarify the scope of the Kubernetes work so the letter cannot be read as claiming cluster-wide operations. Change "built a three-node k3s homelab" or the surrounding professional-project wording to distinguish the environments: "Professionally, I deploy Helm-based test environments with namespace-level access on a shared Kubernetes cluster; personally, I built a three-node k3s homelab..." This is more precise and preserves credibility.
4. In the third paragraph, add the supported AWS evidence because AWS is preferred in the advertisement. After the Terraform sentence, add: "I have also used the AWS free tier for foundational EC2 and S3 learning." Keep the existing statement that Terraform and cloud work have been personal projects; do not imply professional AWS operations.
5. In the final paragraph, replace the phrase "while I continue developing my cloud infrastructure engineering skills" with a more contribution-focused but truthful formulation, such as: "I would bring practical experience in CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test environments, observability and infrastructure automation while continuing to deepen my cloud infrastructure engineering experience." This avoids underselling the candidate while maintaining accurate scope.
6. Do not add claims about Terragrunt, mTLS, production AWS operations, broad network design, security ownership, IoT, or backend engineering. The candidate material does not substantiate those requirements; adding them would reduce the letter's credibility.

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is professional, truthful, well structured, and supported by concrete outcomes: pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes, CI runner costs reduced by approximately 30%, and flaky tests reduced from 7% to below 1%. It clearly explains the candidate’s transition from QA automation toward DevOps and appropriately distinguishes professional Kubernetes experience from personal Terraform and cloud projects. The main weakness is that it spends substantial space describing existing QA/test infrastructure while giving limited direct evidence related to systems architecture, security, networking, and technical leadership—the core focus of this role. The closing also slightly undersells the candidate by emphasizing that they are still “deepening” cloud infrastructure experience.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter uses ATS-readable plain text, standard paragraphs, and relevant supported keywords including CI/CD, GitLab CI, Docker Compose, Helm, Kubernetes, Terraform, GitOps, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik, cert-manager, PostgreSQL, pytest, and Playwright. There are no problematic tables, graphics, headers, or unusual formatting. AI screening probability is moderate rather than high because several prominent job terms are absent or unsupported: Terragrunt, systems architecture, system design, mTLS, networking, security awareness, and stakeholder leadership. These should not be added as claims because the original candidate information does not substantiate them. The letter does mention TLS through cert-manager, but this is narrower than the job’s broader networking and mTLS requirement.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with hands-on infrastructure engineering around CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test environments, automation, observability, Linux-adjacent tooling, analytical improvement, and clear technical documentation. The AWS preference is addressed honestly through foundational personal EC2 and S3 use. The candidate also demonstrates some stakeholder enablement through QA and product review environments, onboarding documentation, ownership of pipelines, and mentoring. However, the candidate’s material shows gaps in strong Terraform and Terragrunt, production cloud environment operation, systems architecture and system design, mTLS and broader network design, practical security, IoT or remote-device integration, and backend/full-stack development. The letter appropriately does not claim these capabilities. The role is therefore a developing or partial match rather than a strong direct match for the stated contractor requirements.
critique.improvement_instructions:
MINOR ENHANCEMENTS:
1. In the third paragraph, make the Terraform scope more concise while preserving the truthful distinction between professional and personal experience. For example, replace “My personal infrastructure projects have given me further hands-on experience with Terraform, Kubernetes and GitOps. Professionally, I deploy Helm-based test environments with namespace-level access on a shared Kubernetes cluster; personally, I built...” with “Professionally, I deploy Helm-based test environments with namespace-level access on a shared Kubernetes cluster. In personal projects, I used Terraform to provision a small Hetzner VPS and built a three-node k3s cluster with Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik and cert-manager.” This reduces repetition and keeps the experience boundaries clear.
2. In the second or third paragraph, explicitly mention Linux because it is supported by the candidate’s original information but currently absent from the letter. For example, add “My foundation also includes Linux, Bash, Python and PostgreSQL tooling” after the sentence describing CI dashboards. Do not add virtual-machine experience, because it is not supported by the candidate’s material.
3. In the final paragraph, replace “while continuing to deepen my cloud infrastructure engineering experience” with a more contribution-focused but still truthful phrase such as “with a strong foundation in delivery infrastructure and a clear focus on developing further in cloud platform engineering.” This avoids unnecessarily weakening the application while not overstating cloud experience.
4. In the final paragraph, use one or two supported terms from the company’s stated culture without making unsupported claims about cultural fit. For example, revise “could contribute to the Fleet Connectivity team” to “could contribute to Corvale’s engineering-led Fleet Connectivity team through practical CI/CD, Kubernetes test-environment, observability and documentation experience.”

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is professional, focused, and credible. It uses concrete achievements, including reducing pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes, reducing CI runner costs by approximately 30%, operating environments for three product teams, and maintaining approximately 900 automated tests. It also handles the candidate's transition from QA automation to DevOps honestly by clearly distinguishing professional Kubernetes experience from personal Terraform and cloud projects. The main content weakness is that the final two paragraphs repeat the same CI/CD, Kubernetes, observability, and infrastructure-automation points rather than using the space to sharpen the strongest evidence of technical ownership and stakeholder impact.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is ATS-friendly: it uses standard paragraphs, no tables or graphics, a clear salutation, and relevant searchable terms such as GitLab CI, Docker Compose, Helm, Kubernetes, Terraform, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Linux, Bash, Python, PostgreSQL, EC2, and S3. It also shows relevant stakeholder impact through infrastructure used by three product teams, QA and product review environments, onboarding documentation, and mentoring. This uses evidence already present in the letter and better matches the requirement to lead technical topics and bring stakeholders along.

Retain one concise closing sentence, for example: "I would welcome the opportunity to contribute practical CI/CD, Kubernetes test-environment, observability, and documentation experience to Corvale's engineering-led Fleet Connectivity team."
